headline: NZ Parliament Advances Environment Ministry Merger Bill Amid Scrutiny Dispute
summary: Parliament voted to advance a bill that would fold the Ministry for the Environment into a new agency covering cities, housing, transport and regional matters, while the Opposition argued the change could weaken environmental oversight and objected to a short scrutiny timetable. Question time focused on employment, health services, homelessness and infrastructure spending, with ministers and opposition MPs disputing both the scale of the problems and the Government’s response. A separate bill to formally recognise English as an official language sparked a heated debate but remained unfinished when the House adjourned.

topicSummaries.topic: Pasifika Unemployment Becomes Flashpoint in Question Time
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Employment and the cost of living affect household security, and the exchange highlighted concerns about economic pressure on Pacific communities and young people.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Carmel Sepuloni challenged Acting Minister for Pacific Peoples Mark Mitchell over figures she cited, including a 12.3 percent Pasifika unemployment rate and an increase of 13,000 unemployed Pasifika people. Mitchell acknowledged that Pasifika unemployment was unacceptably high, but pointed to scholarships, business support, employment programmes and housing initiatives, and argued the Government inherited a weak economy. He did not confirm Sepuloni’s figures, saying he would need to check some numbers.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Carmel Sepuloni (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Did that promise to deliver for Pasifika include delivering a Pasifika unemployment rate of 12.3 percent—more than double what it was when he came into office?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Mark Mitchell (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We recognise that they’re important, that they are serious, and we’re taking it seriously.

topicSummaries.topic: Graduate Nurse Jobs Disputed as Government Cites Lower Vacancy Rates
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The number and placement of nurses can affect waiting times, cancelled procedures and patients’ access to care.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Ayesha Verrall questioned why graduate nurses were missing out on jobs in Christchurch and Tauranga, citing reduced hiring shares and 340 Christchurch graduates who she said had missed out. Health Minister Simeon Brown cited lower nursing vacancy and turnover rates, around 2,000 additional nurses in Health New Zealand since September 2023, and a plan to hire 1,800 graduates this year. The exchange left unresolved the Opposition’s specific questions about graduate placements in the named hospitals.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Dr Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Why did 340 nursing graduates miss out on jobs at Christchurch Hospital, where patients who are nil by mouth, gowned, and minutes away from surgery have their operations cancelled due to lack of staff?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Our Government is making good progress in recruiting the nursing staff that New Zealand needs across New Zealand, in districts up and down this country

topicSummaries.topic: Auckland Homelessness Policy Challenged Over Move-On Orders
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The debate concerns how people living without housing are treated and whether public resources go toward enforcement, accommodation or support services.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Kieran McAnulty asked how move-on orders for homeless people in Auckland would improve housing conditions, while Tamatha Paul raised the potential cost of imprisonment. Finance Minister Nicola Willis, answering for the Housing Minister, said the Government funded transitional housing and support services and would also act on behaviour it said disrupted public peace. Willis did not have figures on how many of 300 announced Housing First places had been filled, offering to provide them later; she rejected McAnulty’s characterisation of the policy as merely presentational.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How will issuing move-on orders, moving homeless people from the CBD to other areas, assist the housing situation in Auckland?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National), on behalf of the Minister of Housing
keyExchanges.quote: It is also the case that, in addition to those social supports available for people, some people behave in ways that are obnoxious and upset the peace of others, and our Government will take action to address that.

topicSummaries.topic: Firefighters’ Pay and Equipment Dispute Continues Through Bargaining
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute affects firefighters’ working conditions and raises public concerns about emergency response capacity and safety.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Lemauga Lydia Sosene questioned whether Fire and Emergency New Zealand could provide fair pay, safe equipment and reliable service while firefighters were striking twice a week. Internal Affairs Minister Brooke van Velden said bargaining had lasted 583 days and was proceeding through facilitated talks at the Employment Relations Authority. She rejected claims that annual funding cuts caused the dispute, citing the cost of a previous pay settlement; the union’s latest proposal, she said, was more than three times the employer’s last offer.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lemauga Lydia Sosene (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How can she be confident when firefighters are striking twice a week?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Brooke van Velden (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Fire and Emergency have been in bargaining with the NZPFU for 583 days. They have been willing to be at the table. Striking doesn’t help settle any faster.

topicSummaries.topic: $56B Roads Estimate Fuels Debate Over Infrastructure Priorities
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Large transport projects compete for public funding with road maintenance and resilience works needed by communities across the country.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Julie Anne Genter said the 17 roads of national significance promoted by National had been estimated at $17 billion but were now understood to cost $56 billion, and questioned the value of the proposed Mount Victoria tunnel works. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the projects had been assessed by the New Zealand Transport Agency and had positive benefit-cost ratios. She said the Wellington project was at an early stage and included more than $1 billion in contingency, while also pointing to a separate programme of resilience works around the country.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Julie Anne Genter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Will she be re-evaluating her Government’s infrastructure priorities, especially the roads of national significance (RoNS), given that the 17 roads the National Party campaigned on, estimated to cost $17 billion, are now understood to cost $56 billion

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: All roads of national significance projects have demonstrated they are value for money in the context of the problems they are trying to solve.

topicSummaries.topic: Environment Ministry Merger Bill Passes First Reading 68–54
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The restructuring will place environmental advice and functions within a larger agency responsible for housing, transport, regional development and local-government functions.
topicSummaries.content: The bill would enable a new Ministry for Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport, combining the Ministry for the Environment with housing and transport ministries and local-government functions from the Department of Internal Affairs. Minister Tama Potaka said the merger would reduce duplication and improve coordination, while environmental functions and statutory responsibilities would remain. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori warned that the environment could lose influence inside a larger, growth-focused ministry. The bill passed its first reading 68–54 and was referred to the Environment Committee. The Government set a 24 April report-back deadline; Opposition amendments seeking later dates were defeated. Commerce Minister Scott Simpson said the timetable was needed for the new ministry to begin on 1 July.

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Tama Potaka (National)
keyExchanges.quote: MCERT will combine key levers across central and local government, reducing duplication and complexity.

keyExchanges.speaker: Lan Pham (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Burying the Ministry for the Environment in a superministry designed to drive development, growth, and infrastructure is the clearest possible signal that this Government can give that the environment comes last.

topicSummaries.topic: English Official-Language Bill Sparks Debate Over Te Reo Māori
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposal has implications for how New Zealand’s official languages are recognised and became a flashpoint in wider debate about identity and national priorities.
topicSummaries.content: Foreign Affairs Minister Winston Peters introduced a bill to formally recognise English as an official language, saying it would clarify the legal position and would not diminish the status of te reo Māori or New Zealand Sign Language. Opponents, including Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori speakers, called the measure unnecessary and raised concerns about its symbolism and effects on te reo Māori. The debate included sharp personal exchanges and was interrupted at the adjournment; no first-reading vote is recorded in the transcript.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill seeks to correct that anomaly, providing consistency in legal framework and clarifying the status of all three official languages in legislation.

keyExchanges.speaker: Oriini Kaipara (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: This bill is a waste of time and a waste of breath.

topicSummaries.topic: 12-Month Prescriptions Introduced for Stable Long-Term Conditions
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Eligible patients may need fewer appointments and repeat-prescription charges, while freeing some GP time for people with more urgent or complex needs.
topicSummaries.content: Health Minister Simeon Brown said patients with stable long-term conditions have been able to receive prescriptions for up to 12 months since 1 February. He said the change applies to conditions including asthma, diabetes, epilepsy and high blood pressure, and could save some patients up to $120 a year. The Government said the policy is intended to reduce routine appointments and improve access to primary care.

keyExchanges.speaker: Sam Uffindell (National)
keyExchanges.quote: How will this change benefit patients with long-term conditions?

keyExchanges.speaker: Hon Simeon Brown (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This is expected to save patients up to $120 per year, for those who receive 12-month prescriptions.

conclusion: The Government secured progress on its agency merger and defended its service and spending record, but sharp disputes over environmental safeguards, public-service pressures and the scope for parliamentary scrutiny remain unresolved.
